scenes.objects: A stored-coordinate line with a position dot inside a dashed ellipse; a fan to three motor-neuron circles; muscle strokes, an eye and a physical-position marker.
scenes.relationship: Shared drive reaches all population cells; private variability enters one example cell; physical variability enters the muscle/eye stage.
scenes.benefit: The fan and collection of outputs show why shared and individual contributions have different routes into movement, while the proposed-source label limits the attractor claim.

scenes.objects: One highlighted lower neuron, one spike-tick record, one recorded-position trace, a pairing bracket, a filter response and a predicted trace.
scenes.relationship: Only the highlighted cell is linked to the spikes. The paired record receives measurement noise. A separate orange dashed calculation takes that one cell through its calibrated filter to predicted eye position.
scenes.benefit: The reader can distinguish what exists physically, what was recorded together, and what was calculated, without mistaking the population drawing for simultaneous neural recording.

scenes.objects: Two same-shape exponential impulse-response filters, alternative input labels, and matched log-lag plots of exact functions.
scenes.relationship: The white-input curve approaches a plateau; the Brownian-position curve keeps growing after passing through the same filter. Separate vertical-axis formulas and a scale note prevent an equal-amplitude reading.
scenes.benefit: The actual plotted shapes show that smoothing alone cannot turn stationary white input into continuing displacement accumulation, while a wandering stored position retains it.

coverage.reason: Local calculation/comparison figure, not an opening map.

items: Input and Position labels in both strips
Same one-pole filter in both strips
claims.reasoning: The two alternatives occur at the filter input. There is no drawn ordinary finite-variance white-noise function and no white-velocity versus Brownian-velocity claim.

claims.evidence: sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD white covariance and MSD; original main p. 10 Eqs. 20-22
claims.reasoning: For unit-gain causal h=exp(-u/tau)/tau, covariance is A exp(-ell/tau)/(2 tau), hence normalized MSD is exactly the displayed function.
Taylor expansion gives x at short lags and limit one at long lags. This is the one-pole result, not the smoother double-exponential kernel used in the paper.
Integrating Cv(s)=D exp(-s/tau)/tau gives 2D tau[x-1+exp(-x)] after the stated velocity transient; normalization is correct.
The function is x squared over two initially and x-1 at long lag, so log slope tends to two then one; no plateau is present.

items: gray dotted x=1 line in each panel
claims.reasoning: Both panels use the same lag variable and axis range; the dotted reference is at one filter time constant.

items: Each panel uses its own scale; physical amplitudes are not matched
claims.evidence: two printed y-axis normalizations; independent covariance calculation
claims.reasoning: The two scales are A/tau and 2D tau, which are different physical quantities. The plots compare shapes without equating input strengths.

items: caption: guide calculation, not measured or fitted paper curves
claims.reasoning: All caption claims match the actual plots and delimit the reconstruction appropriately. The source Fig. 3 and Eqs. 20-22 support the stationary-noise contrast, while the Brownian derivation is explicitly the guide calculation.

items: alt: matched logarithmic lag axes and exact functions
alt: short-lag slopes one/two and long-lag slope one
interpretation: white slope one limited to one-pole model; fuller paper model adds smoother response, motor filtering and feedback
claims.reasoning: The alt describes the plotted functions correctly. The interpretation prevents transfer of the one-pole initial slope to the paper model.

strongest_expert_objection.objection: The white-input initial slope could be mistaken for the paper muscle response, or the two own-scale plots could be taken as equal physical amplitudes.
strongest_expert_objection.resolution: Both filters are explicitly one-pole; the caption identifies a guide calculation and the interpretation limits the short-lag slope. Each y-axis has its own normalization and the image explicitly says amplitudes are not matched. Chapter text also states the stationary-velocity-transient assumption for the Brownian formula.
strongest_expert_objection.verdict: resolved in current image and linked text
